units.translation: And indeed I have resolved: here it runs aground; either for these or for those to raise a great war is all necessity; and the hull is nailed together with ship's windlasses as if brought in.
ship's windlasses: the timbers of ships, in which they are wedged when nailed
turning yourself toward the rising of the sun.
but all other things he turns upside down and sets in place.
to whirl about, to spin. In a figurative sense.
said by tmesis for ὑποστροβεῖ [whirls beneath].
again a terrible pang of true prophecy whirls me about
what opinions are whirling you about?
in what storms we are being whirled about.
Faultily written στρόβους [whirls] for στρόφους [bands]; see under στρόφος.
with a hurricane and rain-beaten squall they went unseen, by the whirl of the evil shepherd.
where in the Preface to the fifth Leipzig edition p. LXXXVIII I emended φάσματα [omens]

φαίνων [showing], having ejected the gloss στρουθῶν [of sparrows]. For neither can φάσματα [omens] placed before στρουθῶν [of sparrows] have the measure of a dactyl, and those little sparrows from Homer Il. 2, 311 ff. flew in here with no less damage to the sense than to the meter: whence Porson already judged that they should be driven away from here. For that Homeric augury is utterly alien to Aeschylus's narrative, which deals with the portent of two eagles in this poem. The scholiast perceived this, who interpreted στρουθῶν [of sparrows] as τῶν ἀετῶν [of the eagles], with about the same right as one might call eagles nightingales or nightingales eagles.
on the right, but blameworthy omens of sparrows.
turning, twist. In a figurative sense, crafty speech, deceits.
the people of the Pelasgians heard persuasive public harangues.
Strophius, father of Pylades, king of Phocis.
where in M is written Στροφίος [Strophios], and likewise sometimes among others cited in the Thesaurus vol. 7 p. 891. The proparoxytone accent is attested by Eustathius p. 1030, 11.
to turn in a circle, to whirl about.
Since Homer said στρεφεδινεῖσθαι [to whirl about], it is more probable that Aeschylus also preferred this to the other: on which L. Dindorf advised in the Thesaurus vol. 7 p. 861.
of birds: high above their nests they whirl about.
girdle: in which sense στρόφιον is more frequent.

where the scholiast: ὦ δυσαδελφόταται πασῶν παρθένων αἳ μίτρας κατὰ τὴν φθορὰν λύονται. ἀντὶ δὲ τῆς μίτρας καὶ ζώνης νῦν στρόφον εἶπεν [O most unhappy of all maidens, who loosen their girdles at their undoing. But instead of the girdle and belt he now said στρόφον].
Thus Spanheim on Callimachus p. 135 corrected for στρόβους [whirls], from the scholiast who explains it as τὰς στροφὰς τῶν ζωνῶν [the twists of the belts].
as many as put a girdle around their garments.
I have girdles and belts, fastenings of robes.
